notes.1:
The exploration, evaluation and subsequent development of an oil and gas reservoir are complex processes which require the integration of the skills and capabilities of a range of technical disciplines. The ultimate objective is to produce a plan for the development of the field and the subsequent implementation of that plan. The process is one of iteration: at the outset the amount of data is strictly limited, and it is only as a result of activities to evaluate the field that data becomes more abundant and a clearer picture is obtained of the reservoir and its production potential.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: identify and discuss the five main stages of field development with their main objectives · identify and discuss the techniques used during the exploration stage · discuss the objectives and required information for reservoir evaluation · identify and discuss the evaluation techniques, including those related to exploration and appraisal wells · identify and discuss the main items considered during design and set-up of facilities · discuss, with a schematic sketch, the various phases of production · discuss the dynamic nature of reservoir monitoring and description in the context of dealing with unique reservoirs.

The five phases

The phases pass from exploration through evaluation and development to subsequent production and depletion, and finally the abandonment of individual wells and the field.

PhaseMain objective
1. ExplorationIdentify the prospect in structural terms: a physical map of the subsurface structure that could act as a trap. Largely conducted by geologists and geophysicists.
2. EvaluationThe nature of the hydrocarbons in place, and the amount in place and the fraction which is recoverable.
3. Design & set-up of facilitiesDesign the reservoir development and evaluate the economics; drill and complete a number of wells; fluid processing and export.
4. ProductionProduce at the maximum rate and for the maximum period possible, safely, at minimum production cost.
5. AbandonmentWhen the well can no longer produce economically, abandon it safely (or use it as an injector or for monitoring).

Chronological basis of field development

The time from initial exploration through evaluation and into development can vary substantially in length depending on the size of the field, its complexity and the environment in which it is likely to be developed.

  • Onshore: the cost of drilling exploration wells and conducting evaluation is relatively low, so it is easier to complete the evaluation in a relatively short time and develop the field. Onshore fields are easier to support logistically but are generally smaller in volumetric extent, requiring less detailed engineering.
  • Offshore: the difficult logistics and the need for more advanced technology may make developments uneconomic unless they are of a substantial size.

Exploration

Objective

The major objective is to identify the prospect in structural terms, i.e. to produce a physical map of the subsurface structure. The aim is to identify a suitable structure which will be likely to act as a trap for the hydrocarbons as they move from the source to the reservoir rock. The structure identification is on a macro scale, since the data available is relatively limited.

Key limitation. There is no attempt at this stage, nor is it possible, to confirm the presence of hydrocarbons within that structure. Indications may come from geological prospects in adjacent blocks or areas where more detailed information is available. The exploration phase yields a geological/geophysical map of the structure showing approximate size and some main features, e.g. faulting. The only means by which the presence of hydrocarbons can properly be evaluated is to physically penetrate the structure and measure and sample the reservoir, which can be done to some extent after drilling the exploration well.

Techniques for identifying a structure

  1. Previous geological / geophysical information. Most reservoirs are in sedimentary basins, so general depositional trends can be used to infer the presence of other reservoir sites. Comparing with adjacent prospects for which more data is already available can be an extremely useful indicator. Sources: private company libraries (maps and drilling, production and well-log data); public agency records, universities, publications; computer-based databases of public and private organisations; general depositional trends from adjacent prospects where more data is available.
  2. Aerial and satellite surveys. Growing use is made of satellites to detect potential subsurface deposits of hydrocarbons and other minerals. Landsat satellites have mapped all of the Earth's landmass, primarily to map vegetation and observe long-term changes on the Earth's surface. The images can be bought from government or companies.
  3. Oil and gas seeps. The most obvious sign. Seepage is often slow, which makes it difficult to detect, since bacteria and weathering may decompose the hydrocarbon as soon as it surfaces. Most such locations have already been exploited.
  4. Geophysical methods. The application of principles of physics to study subsurface geology: measurement of the Earth's magnetism, gravity and especially seismic vibrations, to determine the thickness of sediments and the shape of geological structures. A seismic survey creates an acoustic wave directed into the subsurface. Its movement depends on the density of the strata and on changes in the physical structure of the layers, so the waves are reflected by changes in lithology. The reflected wave is collected and analysed to produce a sectional map of the strata. 3D seismic modelling in particular has contributed substantially to exploration capabilities (see Chapter 3).
  5. Exploration drilling. Based on the geological and geophysical studies, a decision may be made to drill an exploration well, located to intersect the features identified by the geophysics. The cuttings are analysed by the geologist at the well site to build a geological model of the area. As the well is drilled, special logging tools are run before the well is cased. The geological and log data are used to determine whether there are hydrocarbon-bearing zones, i.e. porosity and hydrocarbon fluid saturation. If there are, the nature and quantity of the hydrocarbon, flow properties and pressure of the zone must be assessed, as well as the depth at which the hydrocarbon exists, the thickness of the zone and the presence of an aquifer.

Evaluation

Objectives

  • The nature of the hydrocarbons in place.
  • The amount of hydrocarbons in place and the fraction which is recoverable.

The process of prospect evaluation is expensive and requires considerable technical resources.

Data required

  • Identification of the depositional sequence within the reservoir, and the thickness and mineralogy of the various sediment layers.
  • Data on the pore space: porosity and the fluid saturations.
  • Data on the permeability or production capacity of the reservoir unit.

This list is not exhaustive. Reservoir evaluation requires wells to be drilled to penetrate the structure at several different areal locations, so that data assists more detailed geological mapping of the structure. The process needs inputs from the exploration department as well as drilling and petroleum engineering, and coordination of data collection and acquisition is normally the responsibility of the petroleum engineering department. Drilling exploration wells is generally conducted with specific data-acquisition objectives defined at an early stage, and the cost of exploration wells must in many cases be written off against the value of the data acquired for reservoir evaluation.

Methods built into the exploration well programme

TechniqueWhat it gives
CoringA cylindrical section of the vertical sequence of layers in the reservoir is cut and retrieved for surface evaluation. The principal objectives are a large sample of the reservoir rock, with detailed information on the sedimentary sequence in which the rock system exists.
CuttingsThe pieces generated as a regular bit breaks up the rock. They are fragments and not a continuous sample, so not as useful as cores, but still give useful data on the geology of the formations.
Driller's logThe driller's record of rock and fluid types encountered and the time taken to drill through a particular formation.
Wireline loggingThe second and more important logging source: yields considerable information on the borehole, the near-wellbore reservoir area and the fluid content in that region. Various logging systems are available (see the Logging chapter).
Well testing(1) The presence of mobile hydrocarbons, by inducing the reservoir to produce fluid towards the wellbore. (2) The production capacity of the individual well, in particular the relationship between pressures across the reservoir and flowing.

Well testing in more detail

  • Well tests can be conducted using wireline tools, or using a drill stem or production string to flow-test the well. Testing is expensive but, if designed correctly, can generate information representative of a wider section of the reservoir unit.
  • Repeat formation test. A tool is lowered downhole and positioned against the side of the borehole. It measures the pore pressure (the pressure in the pores of the formation) at that depth and takes a sample of the formation fluid. It is then released and repositioned for another reading; each reading takes a few minutes. The static pressures and depths can be correlated to obtain the density of the fluid (and therefore the type of fluid), fluid contacts, and even information about the reservoir structure. These results do not identify the capacity nor the permeability of the formation.
  • Drill stem tests (DST) (the drill pipe is used as a flow conduit during the test) do identify capacity and permeability. They are very sophisticated tests which allow sections of the formation to flow as though on production. During the test the pressure at the bottom of the well and the flow rates at the bottom or surface are measured. Tests may last 8 to 24 hours, the data (in exploration wells especially) is treated confidentially, and they are very expensive: with the cost of drilling the well they represent a massive investment.

Appraisal wells

The data from the exploration well (even if it was dry) is reviewed and a decision is taken to drill appraisal wells. The object of appraisal well drilling is to delineate the boundaries of the reservoir. In general, if an exploration well has found economically interesting formations, appraisal wells are drilled in succession to the north, south, east and west of the location, ideally to intersect the contacts between oil and water and between oil and gas (if present). The exact location of the wells cannot be planned (or there would be no need for appraisal): the data from each well is reviewed and the location of the next appraisal well changed accordingly. Logging and testing of the appraisal wells is basically the same format as for the exploration well.

Design and set-up of facilities

Once the information from exploration and evaluation has been gained and the reservoir has been modelled to identify the amount of hydrocarbons which can be recovered, the reservoir development is designed and the economics evaluated. Limited data may be available, but if the economics permit, the development proceeds and a number of wells are drilled and completed. During the drilling of the development wells, the wells themselves are evaluated to yield further data on rock and fluid properties at the specific location of each well. In the development drilling phase a considerable component of evaluation is therefore involved, used to improve the reservoir model that will be used to monitor the development. Development both is essential and yields further information, so the development plan can be modified dynamically.

Of particular interest in the development phase:

  • The drilling and completion of individual wells, including the means by which the reservoir is completed across the production interval.
  • Platform requirements for wellhead separation facilities and accommodation.
  • Fluid processing and export systems.
  • The possibility of supporting reservoir production capacity in future by fluid re-injection for pressure maintenance, or of instituting artificial lift at some stage in the life of the reservoir, whereby production of fluids is assisted.

Considerable work is needed to evaluate the development strategy, in particular how the reservoir will respond dynamically, and over an extended period, to production, so considerable technical effort goes into continuously monitoring and improving reservoir production and well performance.

Production

The production phase is intended to allow oil and gas production to proceed:

  • at the maximum rate and for the maximum period possible;
  • with maximum safety in view of the personnel, capital costs and environment;
  • with continuous assessment of the production process to maximise efficiency and ensure minimum production costs.

The production phase is of considerable importance for the overall economics of the development, so technical skills must be applied not only to maintain production but to improve the production process and efficiency.

Phases of production

  • Build-up: the initial production build-up to the capacity of the facility as wells are brought on stream (the steps in the figure).
  • Plateau: the reservoir is produced at a capacity limited by the associated production and processing facilities. The economics of such highly front-end loaded projects require production to be brought up to a plateau level as quickly as possible. Different companies work with different plateau lengths and each project has its own duration. Without detailed consideration, it typically corresponds to approximately 10% of recoverable reserves per annum.
  • Decline: there comes a point when the reservoir is no longer able to deliver fluids at this capacity. The decline phase can be delayed by assisting the reservoir to produce, for example by lifting, which involves placing down-hole pumps and gas lift (the dashed "Artificial lift" curve in the figure). The decline phase is often difficult to model and the aim is to delay it as long as possible to remain at the most efficient plateau production.

Not all of these phases may be part of the plan.

Abandonment

The performance of individual wells is continually monitored and periodically assessed to find ways to improve performance and make production more economic. At some stage a point is reached where the well can no longer produce oil or gas economically, i.e. the cost of the well and its production exceeds the revenue from fluid production, and it should be abandoned safely or maybe used as an injector or for monitoring purposes.

Uniqueness of reservoirs

In the early years of oil exploration little attention was paid to the detailed characteristics of the reservoir. It is now recognised that detailed reservoir properties, associated with often complex phenomena, greatly affect field behaviour. Unlocking these characteristics and understanding the governing laws enables reservoir engineers (in combination with other disciplines) to put in place plans ensuring optimised developments. This requires a dynamic approach, as schematically illustrated in Figure 2.

In many other industries the efforts expended on one project can be used to duplicate a similar size unit elsewhere. Such opportunities are not possible in the engineering of a reservoir. The composition of the fluids is unique, the rock characteristics and related properties are unique, and the size and shape are unique and so on.

  • From our perspective the reservoir description is dynamic: over a period of time the reservoir gives up its secrets.
  • From the reservoir's perspective the description is static, except for the changes resulting from the impact of fluid production or injection.
  • The challenge is reducing the time it takes for our dynamic description to match the reservoir's static description.

The reality is shown in Figures 3 and 4: the top structure map for a North Sea gas field with a ten-year gap shows the impact of knowledge gained from a number of wells compared with that interpreted from the one well. Considerable faulting is shown, not as a result of major geological activity over the ten years but of knowledge gained from the data from drilling new wells. The coverage of the reservoir has also changed, affecting the equity associated with the blocks.

This illustrates the early benefits to be gained from drilling a number of exploration wells. The equity agreements are called unitization agreements, and such agreements are shortened when good quality and comprehensive reservoir description data is available. There can never be sufficient description; however the economics of project management will determine when decisions have to be taken based on the description to date. The value of extra information has to be balanced by the cost of delay in going ahead with a project.

Mock test questions

Class test 2024, Q1(i) (2 marks)

Identify a source of data from the exploration well evaluation techniques that can directly be used to determine the reservoir permeability or production capacity; support your choice with a brief reason.

Solution (as given): Well testing (DST or WFT), as during these operations the flow of mobile fluid is measured.

Class test 2024, Q1(ii) (3 marks)

Describe two of five phases of field development and their main objectives.

Solution (as given): (1) Exploration, identifying potential reservoir; (2) Evaluation, identifying prospect reservoir; (3) Development, design & set-up of facilities; (4) Production, maximising efficiency; (5) Abandonment, safety and security.

Past paper 2025, Q7 (5 marks)

Discuss the differences between wireline log and DST, as two exploration well evaluation techniques, in terms of the type of information they can provide.

Solution (as given): A number of wireline log sondes are used to measure and record electrical, radioactive or acoustic properties of formations to obtain static properties of the rock and fluid, whereas in a DST the well (or section of it) is flowed once through the drill pipe to measure, for the first time, bottom hole pressure and flow rate as dynamic properties, as well as real fluid composition.

Model exam 2026, Q1(ii) (3 marks)

Discuss the three criteria for starting coring operation.

Solution (as given): (1) Special depth given by geologist. (2) Increase in penetration rate indicating porous zone. (3) Hydrocarbon indications (from cuttings, and/or oil and gas in the mud). (4) Cutting showing the transition from a caprock to a reservoir rock.
notes.2:
Geology is the science that deals with the origin, history and physical structure of the Earth and its life as recorded in rocks. A petroleum geologist is concerned with rocks that contain enough petroleum to be commercially valuable. Petroleum geoscience covers the branches of geology dealing with the deposition or creation of rocks, their properties and distribution, and the mapping and analysis of subsurface rock layers and petroleum accumulations. The chapter ends with the petroleum play: the source of the hydrocarbons, the migration pathways, the reservoir rock (porous and permeable), the sealing rock (impermeable) and the trap.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: discuss why geology is important for petroleum engineering · discuss the main objectives of petroleum geology · discuss the concept of plate tectonics · explain how the Earth is structured · identify the three rock types and discuss their main features and differences · discuss the process leading to the formation of sedimentary rocks, their main classifications and characteristics · discuss stratigraphy: its main objective, categories and guiding principles · discuss the common geological structures created by faulting and fracturing of rocks · discuss the main elements required for formation of hydrocarbon reservoirs · discuss the petroleum play: how hydrocarbons are created, migrated and accumulated in rocks, including the categories of petroleum trap · recognise that geologists produce interpretations of the subsurface based on available data, which by their nature could be uncertain.

The Earth

The Earth is a complex, ever-changing body. It is tectonically active (parts of the surface move relative to each other) and compositionally heterogeneous (rocks vary greatly in composition from place to place). It is currently accepted that the planet came into being about 4.5 Ga (billion years ago) by accretion of atoms and particles swirling around the early sun. It evolved, by gravitational separation and thermal convection, into a layered planet (Figure 1):

  • A solid iron inner core
  • A liquid iron outer core
  • A mantle divided into the lower mantle (less mobile) and the upper mantle. The upper mantle consists of the transition zone, the asthenosphere (very mobile) and part of the lithosphere (fairly rigid), which also includes the crust.

The Earth's crust is the solid and cool layer at the surface and is composed of two compositionally different kinds of crust:

Oceanic crustContinental crust
CompositionIron rich, denserSilica rich
ThicknessRelatively thin, up to 10 km thickRelatively thick, around 40 km, or up to 70 km in mountainous regions

(Even 70 km is still only 1.0% of the Earth's radius of 6,373 km.)

Heat and radiometric dating

The presence of heavier radioactive elements, especially uranium and thorium, which decay in a complex radioactive series to produce heat, maintains the Earth's temperature higher than would occur by simple cooling from the initially hot Earth. Radioactivity also gives a set of absolute dating techniques: radiometric dating. Unstable isotopes of an element decay at a characteristic decay rate:

$$-\frac{dN}{dt}=\lambda N\qquad\qquad T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

where λ = decay constant for a particular isotope, N = number of radioactive atoms, t = time. For example, 14C (an unstable carbon atom with 8 neutrons and 6 protons) decays to 14N (a stable nitrogen atom), with a decay constant λ equal to 1.21×10-4. The half-life is T½ = ln 2 / λ = 5730 years. Similarly, rubidium decays to strontium, but with a much longer half-life of 4.88×109 years. The radiocarbon decay series provides an absolute timescale for recent geological or archaeological investigations, whereas rubidium-strontium (Rb-Sr) decay provides a timescale for the ancient geological history of the Earth. With the ability to date rocks, the geological record of the Earth's history and its evolution can be interpreted.

Water, air and life

The presence of water at the surface (the hydrosphere) is essential: without it life (the biosphere) could not exist. The biosphere extends a kilometre or so into the subsurface, and organisms (bacteria) can be found alive in oilfield reservoirs. The hydrosphere was created by degassing of solid material in the early Earth and condensation onto its surface, maintained within a critical range of temperature. The atmosphere is the gaseous outer layer, with the ionosphere at the interface with space. The hydrosphere and atmosphere have evolved from being more hydrogen and carbon dioxide dominated to the more nitrogen/oxygen dominated system of today. By 3.8 Ga early (bacterial) life existed in the oceans and by 2.7 Ga the atmosphere contained free oxygen, resulting in an explosion of new life forms that used O2 rather than CO2.

Plate tectonics

The lithosphere (the crust at the surface and a portion of the mantle that is cool and rigid) is split into sections called plates that move towards and away from each other depending on the movement in the underlying asthenosphere (Figure 2). The Earth's solid crust is constantly being moved around by slow convection currents in the asthenosphere. Plate tectonics is a fairly recent theory (established in the early 1960s) to explain the relationship between continents and oceans, more specifically between continental and oceanic crust.

Plate tectonic theory helps explain the current and past distribution of rocks and rock types across the Earth's surface, and the development of geological structures that could enable trapping of hydrocarbons. It enables us to expect certain associations of rock types within a type of basin, or a distribution of structures due to the geological history of that basin over time.

Evidence: magnetic signatures

Evidence for sea-floor spreading and for the movement of continents over time comes from mapping the magnetic signatures in rocks around the world. This method (for age and location of formation) relies on two things:

  1. Magnetic minerals that crystallise or are deposited when the rock is forming are aligned to the Earth's magnetic field, and remain in that position once the rock is solidified.
  2. The Earth's magnetic field periodically switches orientation (normal to reverse), depending on the circulation within the liquid outer core where the field is generated. This has happened numerous times in the past, the last being around 730,000 years ago, and detecting reversals can therefore be a good dating tool.

For oceanic crust rock (formed at mid-ocean ridges) clear magnetic signatures can be detected that are parallel to the spreading axis. For other rock types, samples are measured in the laboratory, and the strength and orientation of the magnetic field enables determination of where the rock was located on the Earth's surface and when it was created.

Plate boundaries

The crust consists of a number (currently around 55) of plates, which may contain either continental crust, oceanic crust, or both. Where plates meet (plate boundaries) they are converging, diverging, or sliding past each other (transform plate boundaries; Figure 3).

BoundaryWhat happensExamples (as given)
DivergentRifting (continental crust) or sea-floor spreading (oceanic crust)Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland
ConvergentMountain chains, or the destruction of ocean basins at subduction zonesHimalayas, Alps, Rockies and Andes; east of the Philippines
TransformLarge and powerful strike-slip faults in continental crust, or smaller transform faults in oceanic crust (which offset mid-ocean ridges)San Andreas Fault

At subduction zones one plate bends downward and is subducted; the overriding plate is crumpled and uplifted to form mountain chains. Trenches form where the plates meet. As the subducting plate descends into the asthenosphere, the increase in heat causes water within the rocks to be released. As the water rises it causes melting of part of the mantle above the subducted plate, and the rising melt creates volcanoes at the surface. Convergent plate boundaries are the sites of most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes.

Minerals and rocks

Mineral: a naturally occurring inorganic element or compound having an orderly internal structure and characteristic chemical composition, crystal form and physical properties. The properties of each mineral are unique and allow us to identify minerals.
Rock: an aggregate of grains or crystals of one or more minerals (granite contains crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica; marble contains crystals of calcite; sandstone contains grains of quartz and other minerals), or a body of undifferentiated mineral matter (e.g. obsidian) or organic matter (e.g. coal).

Rocks are located in the outermost solid layer of the Earth, the lithosphere (litho = rock). Most of the variety is in the crust, where there are three main types: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Hydrocarbons are contained within rocks, in the pore spaces or porosity. Porosity is defined as the total volume of void space within a rock divided by the total volume of the rock (a percentage void space). Porosity will only exist in some types of rock, more commonly in those composed of grains than those composed of crystals.

IgneousMetamorphicSedimentary

Igneous rocks

  • Molten material is sourced from the Earth's interior (from the mantle or asthenosphere, or from melting of previously existing crust).
  • Extrusive igneous rocks (from volcanoes onto the surface) cool relatively fast, so have fine crystal sizes, often too fine to see with the naked eye. They often contain gas bubbles and include lavas (e.g. basalt, andesite, rhyolite) and tuffs (ash deposits).
  • Intrusive igneous rocks (intruded into previously formed rocks) cool slowly, because there is less temperature difference between them and the surrounding rocks at depth, so have coarser crystals that are easy to see: granite, gabbro, pyroxenite, diorite. At relatively high levels in the crust, intruded melts cool relatively fast, forming medium to fine crystals.
  • Bodies that intrude across the stratigraphy are dikes; bodies that intrude along the layers are sills.

Metamorphic rocks

Thermal metamorphism occurs around hot igneous intrusions, while regional metamorphism is associated with deep burial and mountain-building processes. The bulk composition does not change during metamorphism: limestone (calcium carbonate) becomes marble, a quartz sandstone becomes quartzite, and muddy sedimentary rocks become schists and gneisses. At extreme burial and pressure, metamorphic rocks are melted and recycled as igneous rocks.

Sedimentary rocks and basins

Sediments need space in which to be deposited, and for them to be buried to create sedimentary rocks space needs to continually be created. These locations are called basins: regional areas of active subsidence (low areas) where sediments are accumulating. The mechanism for subsidence can be very variable, but always involves some kind of deformation of the Earth's crust, often associated with plate tectonics. Sedimentary rocks are classified based on what they are primarily made up of:

TypeFormed byPermeability / reservoir quality (as given)
Clastic (detrital)Erosion of pre-existing rocks, transport of the particles by water or air, and eventual deposition, burial, compaction and cementation (conglomerates, sandstones, mudstones)Coarser grain sizes often very porous and permeable; finer grain sizes tend to be impermeable
ChemicalDirect precipitation of minerals from water (limestones and evaporites)Crystalline, so impermeable
OrganicAccumulation of the remains of animals or plants (limestones, chert, coal)Limestones can be very porous and permeable; the other types tend to be relatively impermeable

The three types of rock are continually being created and destroyed by the rock cycle (Figure 4). Sedimentary rocks form the majority of hydrocarbon accumulations, mainly in the sand-sized clastic rocks and in limestones with good porosity (void space) and permeability (the ability of the rock to transmit fluids). Clastic rocks are usually composed of fragments of quartz, feldspar and other silica-based minerals and rock fragments, and are often called siliciclastic rocks. Another categorisation common in the petroleum industry is carbonate rocks: rocks composed of carbonate minerals (CaCO3 or Ca(Mg)CO3), like limestones or dolostones, which are usually either organic or chemical sedimentary rocks.

Porosity and permeability

  • The texture of the rock is defined by the grain size, sorting, shape, roundness and packing or arrangement of the grains. The highest porosity is generally found in well-sorted medium to coarse sandstones. Conglomerates are more poorly sorted, which reduces the void space between grains, and mudstones compact so well that the pore spaces are reduced very effectively during burial and compaction.
  • Permeability relies on the size of the pores and on the size of the pore connections (throats, or connectivity), so larger pores with better connection allow higher permeability. Sandstones tend to have the largest connected pore spaces.
  • Cementation and compaction during burial fill the pores and reduce their sizes, so deeply buried rocks and older rocks tend to have lower porosity and permeability than shallow buried rocks.
  • The texture is highly variable due to sedimentary structures, layers or laminae created during deposition by various transport and deposition processes (gravity flows, transport by various strengths of fluid flow, deposition from suspension of the finest particles). These depend on the depositional environment, e.g. rivers (fluvial) versus beaches (shallow marine). Each environment has a typical assemblage of processes, textural types and layer geometries. Bedding or sedimentary structures result in a heterogeneous distribution of porosity and permeability, which affects the design of production strategies.

Stratigraphy

Sediments are deposited in basins over time, in successive layers. The study of the history of deposition (the geological record), based on detailed analysis of these layers, is called stratigraphy (strata = layers, graphy = study). There are different types depending on what data is being analysed:

  • Lithostratigraphy: the rock types.
  • Biostratigraphy: the fossil content (very useful for determining age and depositional environment).
  • Chemostratigraphy: the chemical composition.
  • Magnetostratigraphy: the magnetic signatures.
  • Sequence stratigraphy: the arrangement or grouping of layers into sequences.

Guiding principles

  • "The present is key to the past": the processes that act on the Earth's surface today are the same as those that acted in the past, so we can infer past processes and what the resulting rock units will look like, including what arrangement of strata will occur in a specific depositional environment.
  • Developed in the 17th century by Nicholas Steno: original horizontality (sediments deposited on a "flat" surface, due to gravitational settling); superposition (in undisturbed strata, younger lies on older strata, older at the bottom); original continuity (horizontal strata extend laterally until they meet some obstacle, or taper off or grade laterally into another sediment). Modern stratigraphers recognise that layers can be deposited inclined (usually only a few degrees), and that lateral changes in lithology occur and are important for understanding the depositional environment.
  • Walther's Law (1894): "Lithostratigraphic transitions in a conformable vertical sequence reflect laterally migrating environments". Each adjacent lithology should come from a depositional environment that was adjacent to the previous one. If two lithologies in a vertical succession could not have been deposited in adjacent environments, we can infer that an unconformity (a period of erosion or non-deposition) has occurred between them.
  • Processes act on what is already there: a variation on the law of superposition. All deformation (folding or faulting) of the strata, or intrusions into the strata, must act only on sediments that are already present. We can use these principles to infer a geological history from the relative order of structures affecting the layers (Figure 6).

Gaps in the record

The preserved geological record represents only a small proportion of the total elapsed time, since most sediments are moved on by non-deposition processes of transport, or many layers deposited are removed by later erosion. Small gaps are called hiatus; large gaps (millions of years) are called unconformities:

  • Angular unconformity: associated with tectonic activity deforming sedimentary strata prior to erosion and new layers being deposited.
  • If the strata are parallel, the unconformity is a disconformity (if there is evidence of erosion) or a paraconformity (caused by a period of non-deposition).

Subdivision by time

Chronostratigraphy is the subdivision of rocks by time and geochronology is time itself. Dating techniques (biostratigraphy, isotope dating, magnetostratigraphy and radiometric dating) have allowed a history of the Earth (remember 4.6 billion years!) to be built up and subdivided hierarchically. The coarsest subdivision is all time before around 542 Ma, the Precambrian. These rocks are generally not of interest to petroleum geologists, because their age means the reservoir rocks are of low quality and the lack of concentrated organic matter means a lack of source rocks. At the base of the Paleozoic Era in the Cambrian Period an explosion of life occurred, after which organic-rich source rocks became much more possible and petroleum systems began to develop.

Geological structures

The strata created by deposition of sedimentary rocks are deformed over time by the stress and strain caused during burial or plate tectonic activities. The strain can be plastic (rocks deform without breaking: folding) or brittle (rocks break across layers: faulting or fracturing). Folding, faulting and fracturing are always younger than all the rock layers that they affect. Structural changes like folding and faulting are key to creating the shapes within a layer of reservoir rock that act as traps for hydrocarbon accumulations.

Describing orientation

  • Planar features (beds, faults): dip and strike. Strike is a horizontal line drawn on the angled surface of a plane, recorded as a compass bearing. The dip is at right angles to this line and is the angle between the plane and a horizontal plane, the angle of inclination, measured by a clinometer.
  • Linear features (fold axes, lineations, slickensides): trend and plunge. Trend is the orientation (compass bearing) of the linear feature and plunge is the angle between that feature and horizontal.

Faults and fractures

  • Faults are breakages in the rock mass where there has been significant movement across the fault plane. Fractures are breakages where there has not been significant movement.
  • Faults can be entirely horizontal movement (strike-slip), entirely vertical movement (dip-slip) or a combination (oblique slip; Figure 7).
  • Strike-slip faults are divided into sinistral (left-lateral) or dextral (right-lateral) depending on which direction the block on the other side of the fault plane is moving, imagining yourself standing on one side and looking across the fault line.
  • Dip-slip faults are divided into normal or reverse depending on whether the block overlying the dipping fault plane (the hanging wall) is rising or falling.
  • Standard illustrations show faults as single planar surfaces, which is simplistic: faults frequently occur in sets of related faults, and a fault is often a complex thick zone of deformation and microstructures, a fault zone. This complexity is often responsible for faults having either much higher or much lower permeability than the surrounding rocks, so they can be either conduits for fluid migration or barriers to flow within a reservoir.
  • Faults create traps by offsetting reservoir layers against sealing layers, or by being sealing layers themselves.

Folds

  • Folds occur where the rocks have bent but not broken, and are subdivided into anticlines and synclines (simply upfolds and downfolds).
  • If the fold axis (the line of maximum curvature between the limbs or sides of the fold) is not horizontal, the fold is said to be plunging. Folds can have similar or different lengths of limbs, and different angles away from the axis at the centre. Folds with a vertical limb are sometimes referred to as monoclines.
  • Folds, especially anticlines, create ideal trapping situations since they naturally create an enclosed high spot where hydrocarbons can accumulate against a seal (if the layer above the reservoir is a sealing lithology). Good situations for trapping occur with folds with multiple or changing plunge directions, or domes, which are anticlines without a linear axis.

The petroleum play

Elements required for formation of hydrocarbon

  1. A source of carbon and hydrogen.
  2. A suitable environment for decomposition of organic materials into petroleum.
  3. Porous and permeable rock(s) allowing holding and migration of petroleum.
  4. A local geological trap for commercial hydrocarbon accumulation.

The petroleum play concept describes how to integrate all the information about the subsurface to determine where hydrocarbon accumulations are likely to occur. The aspects, each vital to the success of an accumulation, are: source rock (also maturity); migration (primary and secondary, and timing); reservoir rock; seal rock; trap (Figure 8).

Source rock and maturity

  • Petroleum (both oil and gas) is created by the conversion of organic material buried with rocks under very high pressure and moderate to high temperature (<200 °C). Organic matter with sufficient heat and time converts to kerogen and then to mobile hydrocarbon. At least a kilometre of burial is required, depending on the geothermal gradient (rate of heat increase with depth).
  • Only a small proportion of the rock is organic matter and only a small proportion of that is converted to hydrocarbons, so a relatively large volume of source rock is required. Good source rocks contain more than 5% organic matter: mudrocks deposited in marine or marginal marine (lagoonal) conditions (especially those deposited in anoxic waters), mudrocks from lacustrine conditions (lakes), and coals.
  • Organic matter is only preserved during deposition if the sediments are not exposed to oxygen (which would oxidise the organic matter before burial) and organisms and bacteria that would consume the organic matter are prevented from accessing it. Therefore source rocks are often created in anoxic depositional environments.
  • A source rock is immature if the burial has been insufficient to convert organic matter to hydrocarbons; mature if the correct temperature has been reached and hydrocarbons have been or are being generated; over-mature if the rock has been buried beyond the hydrocarbon generation window and all the organic matter has been converted to graphite.

Migration

  • When hydrocarbons are generated within the source rock this represents a volume expansion, which results in fracturing the source rock, allowing the hydrocarbons to escape. This is called expulsion or primary migration (source rock to surrounding rocks).
  • Hydrocarbon then migrates away from the source rock within the pore spaces in the surrounding rocks, affected by any hydrodynamic flows. Hydrocarbons are lighter than water, so buoyancy determines that they move upwards. This is secondary migration.
  • Hydrocarbons will migrate up until they reach the surface, unless prevented by a seal, a layer of impermeable rock. Even if a seal is encountered, they tend to migrate along under the seal until they reach a point where they can continue upwards, unless the seal is arranged in conjunction with a good quality reservoir rock into a shape which allows hydrocarbons to migrate in but prevents further upwards or sideways migration: a trap.
Timing. In order for an accumulation to be possible, the reservoir, seal and trap must all be formed before the hydrocarbons are generated and migrate from the source rock. If these are created after migration, there is a strong possibility that the hydrocarbons will have been lost prior to the creation of the traps in which they could have been contained.

Fluids in the trap

Oil and gas displace the water that was originally present in the reservoir rocks, but in most rocks some water remains within the pore spaces, often chemically attracted to the surfaces of the minerals around the pores. Hydrocarbon saturation within a full reservoir therefore rarely reaches 100% and usually ranges between around 60 to 90%. Because of the difference in densities of oil, gas and water (brine = salt water, where salt refers to a number of minerals, not just NaCl), the fluids separate vertically: gas (if present) is found in the highest part of the trap, with oil below it and water below the oil.

Types of trap

According to their geologic features traps are stratigraphic, structural, or most likely a combination (Figure 9).

  • Stratigraphic traps are formed during deposition of the reservoir beds, like unconformity or lenticular.
  • Structural traps are created by tectonic processes after deposition of the reservoir beds, like anticline/dome, fault and salt dome plug traps.
  • Combination traps are formed by a combination of those formed during deposition and by tectonic activities.

Folds, faults, lenticular (pinching out of beds), unconformities and salt domes all create good trapping situations.

From data to discovery

Outcrops at the basin margin provide information about rock types, stratigraphy and depositional environments. The large-scale architecture of strata can be determined using geophysics, specifically seismic reflection surveys (next chapter). Geologists create correlations and maps to illustrate an interpretation of the subsurface depositional environments and structural changes, identifying areas where further exploration is more or less likely to be successful (risk maps). Specific locations for further investigation can then be identified (leads), which can require a more detailed seismic survey, or an area worth drilling (prospects). If a well is drilled, well logs and core samples give more detailed information on the local stratigraphy, rock types and rock properties, including reservoir properties (essential to determine whether any accumulation can be produced effectively and economically). If the well finds hydrocarbons this is called a discovery. Any well only provides information about a specific location, so to judge the size and shape of the reservoir we need to infer the distribution of rock bodies detected in different wells. After a discovery the field is appraised: identifying the boundaries, fluid contacts, size and shape of the field, as well as detailed reservoir properties and structural complexities. An economic analysis of the value of the field is prepared, on which a company may decide to proceed to development.

Uncertainty

All maps, correlations and other presented information about the subsurface are based on the interpretation of a geologist or team of geologists working with the available data. The interpretation relies on the quantity and quality of the data available and will probably change with time and additional data. All conclusions based on these interpretations therefore have a certain amount of uncertainty, and all exploration based on these conclusions has associated risk. Managing and quantifying these risks is an important part of assessment, exploration and reservoir management in the hydrocarbon industry.

Geophysics is the application of principles of physics to the study of subsurface geology. Geophysical methods can be used to measure the thickness of sediments and the shape of structures within sediments. Geophysical prospecting is an essential part of a systematic exploration programme: surveys usually follow the geological survey and precede drilling. When surface geology gives evidence of structure, geophysical methods are often used to confirm the continuation of the structure at depth. When surface indications are absent, as in swamp-covered country, desert and marine areas, or where surface structures are believed to differ markedly from structures at depth, geophysical prospecting provides the only practical means of exploring the area.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: identify and discuss the different geophysical methods and what they measure · identify the rock types and characteristics identified by magnetic and gravity surveys · discuss the importance of seismic survey compared to magnetic and gravity surveys · identify the main output of a seismic survey, its working principle and the important characteristics/properties of acoustic waves · identify the three types of seismic survey and discuss their main differences · compare land and marine surveys and the tools used to create sound waves · perform calculations using the equations for sound velocity (frequency, wavelength), reflection coefficient, acoustic impedance and two-way time, as in the model exam and the tutorials.

Geophysical methods

MethodMeasures
Magnetic surveysThe anomalies in the Earth's magnetic field produced by the magnetic properties of subsurface rocks
Gravity surveysThe anomalies in the Earth's gravitational field produced by the density of the subsurface rocks
Seismic surveysThe time taken for sound waves to travel through rocks

There is no geophysical method which can directly measure the presence of oil in subsurface rocks. Surveys divide into two broad categories:

  • Reconnaissance surveys to outline possible areas of interest where there are thick sediments and the possibility of structural traps.
  • Detailed surveys to define well locations to test specific structures.

Gravity and magnetic surveys are generally regarded as reconnaissance methods. Seismic surveys can be used for reconnaissance and are almost invariably used for detailed surveys.

Magnetic surveys

The igneous and metamorphic rocks of the basement complex are magnetic to varying degrees and create anomalies in the Earth's magnetic field. Sedimentary rocks are practically non-magnetic, so magnetic measurements on or above a sedimentary basin are separated from the source of the anomalies by the thickness of the sediments (Figure 1). As the magnitude of an anomaly is related to the distance from its source, the method can be used to deduce the thickness of sediments overlying the basement. The major tectonic trends of the basement may also be revealed. Lava flows and igneous intrusions usually have quite strong magnetic effects, so their presence in sediments can be detected.

  • The Earth's magnetic field is very weak, varying from 60,000 gammas in a vertical direction at the magnetic poles to about half that intensity in a horizontal direction at the magnetic equator. The field between the poles of a small horseshoe magnet is about 1000 times the strength of the Earth's field.
  • Anomalies significant in oil exploration vary from a few gammas to a few hundred gammas. Magnetometers can measure to a few hundredths of a gamma.
  • Continuous recordings are made of the magnetic field during the survey, and readings from a ground magnetometer ensure there are no magnetic storms during the survey.
  • The results are corrected for variations in the Earth's magnetic field, for errors in the survey procedure and for known regional effects. Maps are constructed with contours to show the anomalies. In favourable circumstances some indication of basement structure may be obtained, along with separation of near-surface and basement effects.

Gravity surveys

Gravity surveys measure the Earth's gravitational field variations due to the density of subsurface rocks. Basement rocks generally have a higher density than the overlying sediments, giving high gravity values when the basement approaches the surface (Figure 2) and low gravity values over depressions in the basement surface. Gravity surveys can therefore outline sedimentary basin development and show structural trends in the basin. Density variations also occur in sedimentary rocks: when older and denser rocks are brought near the surface in the cores of anticlines and other structures, anomalously high gravity values are recorded. The density of salt is usually lower than that of surrounding rocks, and anomalously low gravity values are frequently associated with salt structures such as salt domes.

  • The Earth's gravity field varies from 983.221 gals at the poles to 978.048 gals at the equator. Anomalies of the order of 0.001 gal can be significant in oil exploration, so the unit in gravity surveys is the milli-gal. Gravimeters are sensitive instruments that can measure changes in gravity of 0.01 milli-gal, i.e. one part in one millionth of the Earth's gravity field.
  • The instrument height must be known for each reading, and the procedure is time consuming in rough terrain. Ship surveys house the instrument on a gyroscopically stabilised platform to minimise the movement of the ship.
  • The survey is conducted along a specified number of traverses spaced from 0.5 to 1 mile apart. The readings are corrected for elevation, latitude, topography and diurnal variations and plotted on a map and contoured.
  • The interpretation of anomalies depends on knowledge of the shapes of the subsurface structures. This information is unknown during exploration, so gravity survey data is usually used to provide leads for further geophysical exploration.

Seismic surveys

Seismic surveys provide more detailed information about the shape and depth of subsurface structures than any other method, hence they are the most frequently used. The time taken by the wave to travel from the (man-made) source to the geophones is measured (transferred to electric current) and sent to a seismograph (amplifier and recorder) to produce a seismogram. The travel time depends on the density, depth and mineralogy of the rocks. It rarely takes longer than 6 s and is measured up to 0.001 s. There are normally many changes, also affected by local velocity variation for a particular formation, so interpretation is complicated.

Main outputs: (i) an image of subsurface structure and stratigraphy, (ii) rock (and fluid) properties, (iii) a static reservoir geo-model, (iv) monitoring and updating of the reservoir simulation dynamic model. Seismic surveys give essential input to construct a realistic picture of the underground site, which often requires updating as more information becomes available.

Seismic main working principles

Waves and velocity

Energy released by a sharp sound (e.g. an explosion) is used to construct a picture of underground rock structures. The generated sound waves are composed of a range of frequencies, each with its own power, which for analysis are combined into one using special averaging techniques. As a wave travels through different media frequency (f) is conserved but wavelength (λ) changes as velocity (V) changes:

$$f=\frac{V}{\lambda}$$

Sound velocity changes according to:

$$\begin{aligned}V&=\sqrt{\frac{K+\tfrac{4}{3}G}{\rho}}&&(1)\\ K&=\frac{dP}{dv/v}&&(2)\\ G&=\frac{\text{shear stress}}{\text{shear strain}}=\frac{\text{Force}/\text{Area}}{\text{Transverse displacement}/\text{Initial length}}\end{aligned}$$

where ρ is the density, K (bulk modulus) and G (shear modulus) are rock mechanic properties, v is the volume and P is the pressure. There are two types of wave. Equation 1 is valid for the P (primary or pressure) wave, which has the highest velocity and is mostly used for seismic interpretation. S (shear) wave interpretation is mainly for research purposes.

Reflection

When the wave hits an interface, part of its energy is reflected and part is transmitted. The wave energy reaching the target therefore decreases as it goes through different interfaces. Loss of energy also depends on distance (time) and the properties of the medium, due to seismic dispersion and attenuation. The main contributor for interpreting data and identifying an interface is the reflected energy pattern, expressed by the reflection coefficient between two media:

$$\begin{aligned}R_{12}&=\frac{I_2-I_1}{I_1+I_2}&&(3)\\ I&=V\times\rho&&(4)\ \ \text{acoustic impedance}\end{aligned}$$

As the medium is changed and ρ is altered, velocity can increase or decrease, but the variation of I will be monotonic. Reflection polarity is captured by the sign of R: if I2 > I1 then R > 0 and the reflection polarity is positive. Such a change in polarity assists easier identification of the interface, which is essential to determine different rock type formations.

Depth from two-way time

To estimate the depth of an interface, the known two-way time (TWT), rounded to the nearest 1 ms (0.001 s), is used. For a rock velocity of 4000 m/s this precision equates to $\dfrac{0.001}{2}\times4000=$ 2 m.

$$\text{TWT}=\frac{2d}{V}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d=\frac{\text{TWT}\times V}{2}$$

(d = depth in m, V = wave velocity in the rock in m/s.)

Acquisition: geophones and spreads

  • The reflected energy is recorded by groups of geophones laid on the ground at equally spaced intervals (50 or 100 m apart) along a line. The number of groups used to record each shot may be 24, 48 or as high as 96, so the spread length with 50 m spacing between groups varies from 1200 m to 4800 m.
  • Geophones record all ground movements, so a reflection record is complicated by extraneous movements from natural and man-made sources and from the shot itself. These movements are called noise; they tend to obscure the reflected energy and field techniques are designed to minimise noise and enhance reflections. Noise can be reduced by varying the number and spacing of geophones in a group, using a pattern of shot holes instead of a single shot, and electrical filters in the amplifiers.
  • The greatest improvement in signal-to-noise ratio is obtained by multiple coverage, "common depth point" (CDP) shooting, now almost universally employed on reflection surveys. The shot point and geophone stations are moved along the line between shots, so multiple records are obtained corresponding to reflections from the same subsurface points, i.e. CDPs. The number of stations by which the source and geophone stations are moved between shots determines the multiplicity of cover. The records for each CDP are added during processing to enhance the reflections and cancel out the random noise.

2D, 3D and 4D surveys

SurveyDescription (as given)
2DData acquisition is along a line; gives information on different cross sections of reservoirs.
3DData acquisition is along many parallel lines to form a cubic picture; a large oil volume is expected to justify the cost.
4DA succession of 3D surveys repeated at intervals of time. Used to monitor changes in fluid levels and pressure in the reservoir. This is the one that has received a lot of attention in recent years, mainly as it helps to monitor and update the reservoir simulation dynamic model.

Land and marine surveys

The seismic reflection method can be applied to both marine and land surveying, but the different problems require different operational techniques.

  • Land: the energy source is normally a small explosive charge detonated in a shallow drilled hole, but vibrating plate sources (e.g. a Vibroseis truck, Figure 3) are also available. Vibrating sources have much less energy than a dynamite charge, but adding the signals from repeated vibrations improves the signal-to-noise ratio to compensate. In the old days a falling weight from a truck was also used.
  • Marine: the recording and shooting can be done from a single ship, which houses the recording instruments and tows a neutrally buoyant cable containing the geophones. The energy sources are generally non-dynamite: compressed air or gases exploding under water, or an electric discharge under water. These are towed at the rear of the ship at a suitable depth beneath the sea surface (Figure 4).
  • Under favourable weather conditions surveys proceed much faster at sea than on land, because drilling of shot holes is eliminated and the geophone spread moves continuously along the line. As a consequence, the multiplicity of subsurface coverage recorded on marine surveys is generally higher than on land surveys.

Interpretation of seismic results

The object of a seismic survey is the location and detailing of structural traps in which oil may have accumulated. The initial programme of seismic lines depends on the existing knowledge of the area and may vary from widely spaced reconnaissance lines over an unexplored area to a detailed survey to assist in the location of development wells.

  • When the field records have been processed, the travel times are plotted on maps and contours drawn through equal time values. A separate map is drawn for each formation. The time-contour (isochron) maps show all the structural features, but depth-contour maps are more convenient for exploration purposes.
  • The picking of times to the reflection horizons and the contouring are done by computer, allowing conversion of travel time into depth and hence the production of isopach maps.
  • The velocities used in the conversion of time to depth can vary from about 4000 feet per second for unconsolidated near-surface sediments, to 6000 to 13000 feet per second for sandstones and shales and 14000 to 20000 feet per second for limestone, so it is essential to determine the appropriate velocity for each area. Significant velocity variations in an area can cause an appreciable change in the shape of the contours as they are converted to depth. Table 1 gives the sound velocity in some typical rocks.
  • Measuring velocity: the direct method is to lower a geophone into a well and measure the travel times from shots near the surface to various depths in the well. However velocity information is frequently required before the first well is drilled and can be obtained from a statistical analysis of seismic data. When a well has been drilled a continuous velocity log may be run to confirm the velocity values; it measures and integrates travel times over short portions of the well, and the accuracy of the integration is checked at selected depths against travel times measured directly with a geophone.

The underground reserves of oil and gas form the oil company's main assets. Quantifying such reserves is therefore a very important objective of the practising reservoir engineer, but also a very complex problem, for the basic data is usually subject to widely varying interpretations and reserves may be affected significantly by the field development plan and operating practice. It is an on-going activity during exploration, development planning and production, and a key task of the appraisal phase, for it is at the heart of determining project viability.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: discuss the concept of reserve, the deterministic and probabilistic methods of reserve estimation, the uncertainty associated with reserve calculation and its variation during reservoir production life · discuss and show the probability versus recoverable reserves indicating proven, proven + probable and proven + probable + possible reserves · present and use the given equation for the volume of oil in place · understand the impact of uncertainty on reserve during the production life · perform calculations to obtain reserve estimates, as in the model exam and tutorials.

Introduction: the volumetric estimate

Before any production has been obtained, the so-called volumetric estimate of reserves is usually made. Geological and geophysical data are combined to obtain a range of contour maps, with the help of a planimeter and other tools, to estimate the hydrocarbon-bearing rock volumes. From well-log petrophysical analysis, estimates of an average porosity and water saturation can be made, and applied to the hydrocarbon rock volume they yield an estimate of oil in place (STOIIP). Only a fraction of this oil may in fact be "recoverable", so laboratory tests on cores may be carried out to estimate movable oil. The reserve estimate finally arrived at is little more than an educated guess, but a very important one, for it determines company policy. In 1987 the Society of Petroleum Engineers, in collaboration with the World Petroleum Congress, published definitions with respect to reserves; these are now accepted world-wide.

Reserve definitions

Reserves are those quantities of petroleum which are anticipated to be commercially recovered from known accumulations from a given date forward.
  • All reserve estimates involve some degree of uncertainty. The uncertainty depends chiefly on the amount of reliable geologic and engineering data available at the time of the estimate and the interpretation of that data.
  • The relative degree of uncertainty may be conveyed by placing reserves into one of two principal classifications: proved or unproved. Unproved reserves are less certain to be recovered than proved reserves and may be sub-classified as probable and possible to denote progressively increasing uncertainty in their recoverability.
  • Because of potential differences in uncertainty, caution should be exercised when aggregating reserves of different classifications.
DeterministicProbabilistic
MethodA single best estimate of reserves is made, based on known geological, engineering and economic data. Volumes are determined by calculating values for the various parameters.The known geological, engineering and economic data are used to generate a range of estimates and their associated probabilities, using statistical analysis with tools like Monte Carlo methods.

Figure 1 gives a schematic of reserves showing the progression with time (reserve categories at the P10, P50 and P90 probability levels, from potential before drilling through the SPE/WPC definitions to abandonment).

The curve in Figure 2 presents the probability that the reserves will have a volume greater than or equal to the chosen value. On this curve:

  • The proven reserves represent the reserves volume corresponding to 90% probability (P90) on the distribution curve.
  • The probable reserves represent the volume corresponding to the difference between 50 and 90% probability.
  • The possible reserves represent the volume corresponding to the difference between 10 and 50% probability.

Volume in-place calculations

The estimate of reservoir volumes can be accomplished by a number of techniques, largely based on material balance, or reservoir volume estimations by mapping the subsurface contours of the reservoir. The volumetric methods involve determination of the bulk reservoir volume, average porosity and fluid saturations, which leads to the total volume of hydrocarbon in the reservoir. The volume recoverable is estimated by applying a suitable recovery factor and the appropriate formation volume factor:

$$\text{Recoverable oil}=\frac{V_b\times\phi\times(1-S_w)\times RF}{B_o}\qquad(1)$$
SymbolMeaning (as given)
Vbbulk reservoir volume (Res. bbl)
φfractional porosity (Frac.)
(1 - Sw)hydrocarbon saturation (Frac.), assuming the only fluids present are water and hydrocarbon such that their saturations must sum to one
RFrecovery factor (Frac.)
Boformation volume factor for oil (Res. bbl/STB)

The recovery factor is determined approximately by considering: (a) a laboratory measurement of oil displacement in cores, the residual oil saturation; (b) the type of displacement mechanism involved; (c) a correlation of sweep efficiency based on a similar reservoir.

Probabilistic representation of reserves

As with the deterministic approach there is also some measure of subjectivity in the probabilistic approach. For each of the elements in Equation 1 there is a probability function expressed in low, medium and high probabilities for the particular values. Figure 3 shows a possible distribution scenario for each of the elements (net rock volume Vnr, net rock average porosity φ, connate water saturation Swc, formation volume factor Bo, estimated recovery factor RF) and the final result.

The resulting calculations give a probability function for a field, as shown in Figure 4, where the values for the three elements are:

  • Proven = 500 MM stb (the P90).
  • Probable = 240 MM stb, which together with the proven makes up the P50 of 740 MM stb.
  • Possible = 120 MM stb, which together with the proven-probable gives the P10 of 860 MM stb.

As a field is developed and the fluids are produced, the shape of the probability curve changes. Probability figures for reserves are gradually converted into recovery, leaving less uncertainty with respect to the reserves (Figure 5). Reserves estimates are generally revised as additional geologic or engineering data becomes available or as economic conditions change.

Reserve estimate during reservoir life

Reserves usually become less uncertain with time as production continues and more reliable information is obtained. However, reserve is needed even at an early stage in reservoir planning, and it is necessary to consider how departure from the available "best estimate" of the essential reservoir parameters will affect the viability of the project if the reserves are significantly greater or smaller than the "central estimate". The effect of the sensitivity of the reserve estimate can be approached in a probabilistic manner by estimating the spread of results for one particular parameter about a mean value. The spread can be assessed by, among other techniques, a Monte-Carlo simulation, which is beyond the scope of this course. The estimate of reservoir volume is required at various stages in a project:

StageEstimate (as given)
Geophysical exploration stagesSome order-of-magnitude estimate of the reserves which a structure might contain is necessary to rank the probability of economic success of various projects prior to making bids. The first estimate is based on the volume of the structure determined from seismic maps, supplemented by information on local geological trends which may indicate the thickness of porous beds. By applying the common range of rock parameters, porosity (7% to 30%), water saturation (8% to 40%) and recovery factor (10% to 50%), a possible range of reserves is estimated.
Exploration stageWith the drilling of a discovery well, the uncertainty of encountering hydrocarbons is removed, and measured values for porosity and water saturation become available for the section of reservoir encountered. Assuming the well log data corroborate the prior seismic data, now only the contour of the hydrocarbon/water contact (OWC) is required to make a reasonable estimate at this stage.
Field development stageAs new wells are drilled, the volume and geometrical distribution of the reservoir become even more accurately defined, as well as the average reservoir porosity and saturation values. However, fluid injections and withdrawals into the reservoir and the corresponding changes in fluid interfaces must be accounted for as the inventory of reserves is continuously upgraded. Whether the accounting is made by computer or manually, the procedures are the same in principle.
