The pore pressure of a fluid within a rock pore space is developed as a result of physical, chemical and geologic processes through time over an area of sediments. Determining the magnitude and variation of pressures in a reservoir is an important aspect in understanding various aspects of the reservoir, during both the exploration and production phases.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: identify and discuss lithostatic pressure, hydrostatic pressure and pore pressure · identify and discuss normal pressured, overpressured and underpressured reservoirs · state, supported with a schematic sketch, the equations describing normal pressured, overpressured and underpressured reservoirs · discuss the causes of abnormal pressure · discuss the normal reservoir temperature concept · perform calculations to obtain reservoir temperature and reservoir pressure within the water, oil and gas zones, as in the model exam and tutorials.

Lithostatic and pore pressures

Oil and gas accumulations are found at a range of sub-surface depths. At these depths pressure exists as a result of the depositional process and from the fluids contained within the porous media. These pressures are called lithostatic pressures and fluid pressures (Figure 1).

  • The lithostatic (sometimes called geostatic or overburden) pressure is caused by the pressure of rock which is transmitted through the subsurface by grain-to-grain contacts. It is of the order of 1 psi/ft. The gradient varies according to depth, the density of the overburden, and the extent to which the rocks are supported by water pressure. Using the gradient of 1 psi/ft, the geostatic pressure Pop in psig at a depth of D in feet is Pop = 1.0 D psig.
  • The geostatic pressure is balanced in part by the pressure of the fluid within the pore space, the pore pressure, and also by the grains of rock under compaction.
  • In unconsolidated (loose) sands the overburden pressure is totally supported by the fluid, and the fluid pressure Pf is equal to the overburden pressure Pop.
  • In deposited formations like reservoir rocks the fluid pressure is not supporting the rocks above but arises from the continuity of the aqueous phase from the surface to the depth D in the reservoir. This fluid pressure is called the hydrostatic pressure: imposed by a column of fluid at rest, with a value that depends on the density of the water ρw, which is affected by salinity. In a sedimentary basin, where sediment has settled in a region of water and hydrocarbons have been generated and trapped, we expect a hydrostatic pressure for a continuous column of water: Pf = ρw D g, where g is the acceleration due to gravity.
  • There is another fluid pressure which arises from fluid movement. This does not contribute to in-situ pressures at rest, which is the focus here.

Fluid pressure in hydrocarbon accumulations is dictated by the prevailing water pressure in the vicinity of the reservoir. In a normal situation the water pressure at any depth is:

$$p_w=\left(\frac{dp}{dD}\right)_{\!w}D+14.7$$

where $\dfrac{dp}{dD}$ is the hydrostatic pressure gradient. This equation assumes continuity of water pressure from the surface and constant salinity. In most cases, even though the water-bearing sands are divided between impermeable shale, any break of such sealing systems will lead to hydrostatic pressure continuity, but the salinity can vary with depth. Reservoirs whose water pressure gradient, when extrapolated to zero depth, gives an absolute pressure equivalent to atmospheric pressure are called normal pressured reservoirs.

Hydrostatic pressure

Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure exerted by water at any given point within the fluid at rest, generated by the density of the fluid and the vertical height of the fluid column:

$$P=\rho_w\,g\,h\qquad\rho g\ \text{is a force/volume term:}\quad\frac{\text{force}\times\text{depth}}{\text{volume}}=\frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{m}^3}=\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^2}=\text{Pa}$$

In imperial units the ρg term is usually quoted in lb/gal. To convert to psi/ft use 1 ft³ = 7.48 gal and 1 ft² = 144 in²:

$$1\ \frac{\text{psi}}{\text{ft}}=1\ \frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\times7.48\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{ft}^3}\times\frac{1}{144}\ \frac{\text{ft}^2}{\text{in}^2}\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\frac{1\ \text{psi/ft}}{1\ \text{lb/gal}}=0.0519$$

E.g. fresh water with a density of 8.34 lb/gal exerts a pressure of 8.34 × 0.0519 = 0.433 psi/ft. Water salinity changes this value, e.g. 0.45 psi/ft for saline water of 55,000 ppm. In a vertical column of this fluid, the pressure at any depth is 0.433 psi greater for each foot of depth. The typical densities of common reservoir fluids are in Table 1.

Table 1: Typical reservoir fluids density.

Overburden stress (pressure)

Overburden pressure (or stress) at any point in the formation is the pressure exerted by the total weight of the overlying formations:

$$\begin{aligned}s&=\int_0^{z}\rho(z)\,dz\\ s\ (\text{psi})&=0.433\int_0^{z}\rho(z)\,dz\end{aligned}$$

(ρ in g/cm³, z in feet; 1 g/cm³ = 0.433 psi/ft.)

where s is the overburden pressure, z is the depth interval and ρ is the bulk density. Bulk density is a function of rock matrix and fluid density and porosity:

$$\rho_b=\phi\rho_f+(1-\phi)\rho_m$$

(ρb = bulk density g/cm³; ρf = pore fluid density (g/cm³); ρm = matrix density (g/cm³).) If porosity approaches 0, ρb approaches ρm. As porosity approaches 1, ρb approaches ρf. The approximate bulk density of a thick sequence is 2.3 g/cc or 1 psi/ft. Onshore the overburden gradient may be close to 1 psi/ft, but offshore it may be lower, 0.7 psi/ft, due to sea depths, air gap etc. Typical rock densities are in Table 2.

Table 2: Typical reservoir rocks density.

Abnormal pressure

Under certain conditions fluid pressures may depart substantially from the normal pressure. Overpressured reservoirs are those where the hydrostatic pressure is greater than the normal pressure, and underpressured reservoirs are below normal pressure (see Figure 1). They are called abnormally pressured reservoirs and can be defined by the equation:

$$p_w=\left(\frac{dp}{dD}\right)_{\!w}D+14.7+C$$

where C is a constant, positive for overpressured and negative for an underpressured system. For abnormally pressured reservoirs the sand is sealed off from the surrounding strata so that there is no hydrostatic pressure continuity to the surface.

Factors influencing abnormal pore pressure generation

  • Thermal effects, causing expansion or contraction of water which is unable to escape; an increase in temperature of 1 °F can cause an increase of 125 psi in a sealed fresh water system.
  • Clay diagenesis. Montmorillonite diagenesis to illite produces water from the clay particles as they compact. The water increases the fluid pressure if it cannot escape. Clay can react with water different from the one it had originally created.
  • Osmosis. Clay acts as a semipermeable membrane across which water may flow if there are different salt solutions on either side of the barrier. Two related phenomena are electro-osmosis (chemical reactions cause an electric potential and water movement) and thermo-osmosis (related to the temperature difference across the barrier).
  • Tectonism. Tectonic geological forces can deform or displace sediments depending on the regional stress and the subsequent structural development. The new position of sediment in a fold or fault will indicate a pressure different from that corresponding to the original depth.
  • Rapid burial of sediments consisting of layers of sand and clay. The speed of burial does not allow fluids to escape from the pore space.
  • Depletion. Production from the reservoir, natural or man-made.

Pore pressure calculation

To determine pressures within gas, oil and water fluid regimes, consider Figure 2, the diagram of a normally pressured reservoir sequence. The depth to the oil-water contact is x; the depth to the gas-oil contact is y. The depth of interest is h.

Assumptions: pores of all sediments are filled with water in the Earth; pores are all interconnected; transition zones between fluids (oil/water, gas/oil, gas/water) are relatively small. The change in pressure is dp = ρ g dh, where $\dfrac{dp}{dh}$ is the hydrostatic pressure gradient. If p1 is the pressure at h1, p2 is the pressure at h2 and ρ does not change much with depth, p2 - p1 = ρ g (h2 - h1). The following formulae for initial hydrostatic pressures are then applicable.

$$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Water filled pores}\qquad p_w-p_{\text{surface}}&=\rho_w\,g\,h\\ \textbf{Oil filled pores}\qquad p_o(h)-p_o(x)&=\rho_o\,g\,(h-x)\\ \textbf{Gas filled pores}\qquad p_g(h)-p_g(y)&=\rho_g\,g\,(h-y)\end{aligned}$$

pw = pressure at depth h; psurface = pressure at depth 0 (surface), mean atmospheric pressure. po(x) is the pressure at the oil/water contact and po(h) the pressure at any depth h. pg(y) is the pressure at the gas/oil contact and pg(h) the pressure at any depth h.

The density of formation water, ρw, does vary with depth because of different water salinities. However, it can be fixed by using an average value, for instance by measuring pressure at 2 depths. If there is no difference in pressure at the oil/water contact and the oil/gas contact, then pw(x) = po(x) and po(y) = pg(y), so:

$$\begin{aligned}p_o(h)&=p_{\text{surface}}+\rho_w g x+\rho_o g(h-x)\\ &=p_{\text{surface}}+(\rho_w-\rho_o)g x+\rho_o g h\\ \text{i.e. } p_o(h)&=\rho_o g h+\text{constant}\\[8pt] p_g(h)&=p_{\text{surface}}+\rho_w g x+\rho_o(y-x)g+\rho_g(h-y)g\\ &=p_{\text{surface}}+(\rho_w-\rho_o)g x+(\rho_o-\rho_g)g y+\rho_g g h\\ \text{i.e. } p_g(h)&=\rho_g g h+\text{constant}\\[8pt] \text{Similarly for a GWC (depth } z\text{):}\quad p_g(h)&=p_{\text{surface}}+(\rho_w-\rho_g)g z+\rho_g g h\end{aligned}$$

Pore pressure measurement

Indirect methods

These give an indication of pressure values and are treated as qualitative rather than quantitative (the direct methods are described in the next section):

  • Surface pressures during a kick, the flow of reservoir fluid into the well during drilling. It is unlikely that the company will drill for a kick just to measure pore pressure.
  • Log-derived fluid densities, which give the fluid pressures.
  • Velocity analysis of seismic data, to indicate formation compaction.
  • Mud density/gas relationship: the differential pressure affects the amount of formation gas entering the mud.
  • Cuttings nature, i.e. the fragmentation and nature of the cuttings.
  • Drilling exponents determine the drillability of the formation, which is affected by the differential pressure across the bottom of the hole, so pore pressure may be determined from drilling exponents.
  • Shale density: by rapid determination of shale density, the trends of shale density of the section the drill is cutting through can be determined.

Direct technique

The first generation of vertical pressure logging tools, introduced in the mid-1950s, could take one fluid sample and measure one formation pressure. They were succeeded by Repeat Formation Testers (RFT), introduced in 1975, capable of acquiring two fluid samples and unlimited pressure measurements, which constitute the distributed pressure data. Since then significant advancements have been achieved in tool design, operation and data analysis techniques, particularly to obtain more representative reservoir fluid samples and in hardware mechanical reliability, enhancing the pressure measurement quality especially in challenging environments. Over the years the main application is to provide pressure-depth profiles over reservoir intervals.

The RFT device places a probe through the well mud cake and allows small volumes of fluid to be taken and pressure measurements to be made (Figure 3). It can therefore only be operated in an open hole environment. The unit can be set at different locations in the well and the pressure gradient thereby obtained. The pressure-depth survey can be used to obtain fluid gradients, fluid contacts and particularly reservoir characterisation, aiding improved reservoir management decisions leading to optimum production.

Reservoir temperature

The temperature of the Earth increases from the surface to the centre. The heat flow outwards through the Earth's crust generates a geothermal gradient. This temperature variation conforms to both a local and regional geothermal gradient, resulting from the thermal characteristics of the lithology and the more massive phenomenon associated with the thickness of the Earth's crust along ridges, rifts and plate boundaries.

  • In most petroleum basins the geothermal gradient is of the order of 1.6 °F/100 ft (0.029 K/m).
  • The thermal characteristics of the reservoir rock and overburden formations give rise to a large thermal capacity, and with a large surface area in the porous reservoir one can assume that flow processes in a reservoir occur at constant reservoir temperature.
  • The local geothermal gradient is influenced by associated geological features like volcanic intrusions etc. It can be deduced from wellbore temperature surveys, which have to be made under stabilised conditions, since they can be influenced by transient cooling effects of circulating and injected fluids, which can be corrected by proper analysis of the measured data during or immediately after drilling.

Without temperature surveys, the temperature at a vertical depth (D) can be estimated using a typical geothermal gradient and a surface temperature of 15 °C (60 °F), using:

$$T_{(D)}=288.2+\mathrm{T.G}\times D\qquad(\text{K})$$
